strengths: Achieves a new state-of-the-art FID (1.61) among pixel-space generative models on ImageNet 256x256, substantially narrowing the historical gap to latent diffusion models while using markedly less compute (311 GFLOPs) than most other pixel-space baselines (hundreds to thousands of GFLOPs), as shown in Table 11.

Demonstrates, to the authors' knowledge, the first purely transformer-based pixel-space diffusion model trained end-to-end at 1024x1024 resolution for text-to-image generation, which is a meaningful scalability contribution given prior pixel methods have struggled at such resolutions.

The dual-level architecture (patch-level DiT + pixel-level PiT with pixel-wise AdaLN and pixel token compaction) is a sensible, well-motivated design to address the core computational bottleneck of dense per-pixel attention, and the paper clearly explains the mechanism (compress-attend-expand) and its rationale.

Extensive and systematic ablations are provided, both in the main text and appendix: component-wise ablation (Table 4), token compaction rate study (Fig. 10), patch-size and model-size scaling (Fig. 5, Fig. 9 depth allocation), sampler comparison (Fig. 7), CFG scale/interval study (Table 8), and FLOPs comparisons (Table 11), giving a fairly complete picture of design choices.

Qualitative results are strong and diverse (class-conditional ImageNet samples, high-resolution T2I samples, uncurated samples in the appendix), and the paper also shows a practical downstream benefit—better detail preservation in training-free image editing—by avoiding VAE reconstruction artifacts (Fig. 1b).

Quantitative T2I results (GenEval 0.74, DPG-Bench 83.5 at 1024^2) are competitive with several established latent diffusion baselines despite using a comparatively small model (1.3B) and modest training data (~26M pairs), suggesting the architecture is reasonably parameter/data efficient.
weaknesses: Despite the improvements, PixelDiT still trails the strongest latent diffusion models on ImageNet FID (1.61 vs. 1.13 for RAE-XL and 1.26 for DDT-XL), so the central motivating claim (that pixel-space training can match or surpass latent methods) is only partially substantiated; the paper is careful to frame this as 'narrowing the gap' but the gap remains non-trivial.

The image-editing advantage (Fig. 1b) is illustrated with a single qualitative example rather than a quantitative benchmark (e.g., editing fidelity/consistency metrics over multiple prompts and images), which limits the strength of this claimed contribution.

Details of the 26M image-text pair pretraining corpus for the T2I model (source, curation, caption quality/generation process, licensing) are not disclosed, which raises reproducibility concerns and makes it hard to judge whether reported T2I gains stem from architecture versus data curation.

No code/data release is mentioned, and some architectural specifics (e.g., exact linear projection dimensions for pixel-wise AdaLN, memory overhead of the per-pixel modulation MLP) are only partially quantified, which could hinder exact reproducibility.

T2I evaluation relies solely on automatic benchmarks (GenEval, DPG-Bench); no human preference study or standard FID-based image-quality comparison (e.g., on COCO) is reported, leaving open questions about perceptual quality relative to competing latent T2I systems.

Training cost (wall-clock/GPU-hours) for both ImageNet (up to 1.6M iterations) and T2I pretraining/finetuning stages is not reported, making it difficult to fully assess the practical efficiency trade-off against latent models beyond the FLOPs-per-forward-pass metric.

strengths: Strong empirical results: PixelDiT-XL achieves 1.61 gFID on ImageNet 256x256 and 1.81 on 512x512, clearly outperforming prior pixel-space generative models (PixelFlow, PixNerd, EPG, JiT) and even surpassing some latent-space models (e.g., REPA-SiT), which is a notable result for pixel-space diffusion.

The dual-level architecture (patch-level DiT for global semantics + pixel-level PiT for per-pixel refinement) with pixel-wise AdaLN and pixel token compaction is a clean, well-motivated design that directly addresses the O(N^2) attention cost of dense pixel tokens while retaining per-pixel fidelity.

Extensive and careful ablations (Table 5/6, depth allocation N/M, compaction rate, patch size, REPA necessity, solver comparison, guidance scale/interval sweeps) substantiate the individual design choices rather than just reporting end results.

Scalability is demonstrated convincingly: the model is extended to 1024x1024 text-to-image pretraining directly in pixel space, achieving competitive GenEval (0.74) and DPG-Bench (83.5) scores against strong latent diffusion baselines (SDXL, PixArt, FLUX), which is a substantial engineering and scientific achievement.

The image-editing experiment (FlowEdit) convincingly demonstrates a genuine practical advantage of pixel-space diffusion — avoiding VAE reconstruction artifacts — supported by quantitative background-preservation metrics (MSE/SSIM) in addition to qualitative examples.

Unusually transparent reporting of negative/failed results (Appendix G: factorized AdaLN, Haar wavelet pretransform, alternative conditioning mechanisms, x-prediction instability, encoder-decoder bottleneck) adds scientific value and reproducibility insight beyond the typical paper.
weaknesses: Some claimed architectural novelty (pixel-wise AdaLN, dual-level patch/pixel decomposition, token compaction) has close conceptual overlap with existing pixel-space works cited in the paper (e.g., PixNerd's neural field layers, U-ViT-like hierarchical designs, EPG), and the paper's distinction from these concurrent works is described somewhat briefly rather than analyzed in depth.

Despite strong results, PixelDiT-XL (1.61 gFID) still does not surpass the very best latent models overall at comparable epoch counts in every setting (e.g., RAE-XL 1.13 gFID at 800 epochs vs. PixelDiT-XL 1.61 at 320 epochs, though extended training to 800 epochs only reaches 1.54), so the 'closing the gap' claim, while true, leaves residual gap that could be stated more precisely.

Reported throughput/efficiency comparisons (e.g., samples/sec at 1024^2) are only benchmarked against a narrow set of methods and lack direct wall-clock/memory comparisons against strong latent T2I baselines (SDXL, FLUX) at the same resolution, making the efficiency trade-off versus latent models less clearly quantified.

The text-to-image training data description is very brief (only ~26M image-text pairs, no details on data curation/filtering/licensing), which limits reproducibility and makes it hard to assess how much of the T2I performance stems from data quality versus architecture.

The paper acknowledges training instability (loss spikes with velocity prediction, especially for deeper/longer runs) as an open, unresolved issue, which is a real limitation for practical adoption and reproducibility of the training recipe.

Some quantitative comparisons in Table 4 mix models of different parameter counts and training data scales (e.g., FLUX-dev at 12B vs. PixelDiT-T2I at 1.3B), so while impressive, the comparison somewhat overstates parity with 'best latent diffusion models' given the large capacity gap.

strengths: The proposed dual-level architecture (patch-level DiT for global semantics + pixel-level PiT for local detail) is a well-motivated and technically clean solution to the quadratic-cost problem of dense pixel-space attention, and is clearly explained with supporting diagrams (Fig. 2-3, 7).

The two key mechanisms -- pixel-wise AdaLN modulation and pixel token compaction -- are original contributions that meaningfully differ from prior patchification or cascaded pixel-diffusion approaches, and their necessity is directly demonstrated via a careful component-wise ablation (Table 5) showing large gFID improvements at each step and an OOM result when compaction is removed.

Strong quantitative results: PixelDiT achieves state-of-the-art FID among pixel-space generative models on both ImageNet 256x256 (1.61) and 512x512 (1.81), and even surpasses some competitive latent diffusion baselines (e.g., REPA, gFID 2.08) without using any autoencoder, which is a nontrivial empirical result.

The method is shown to scale to text-to-image generation directly in pixel space at 1024x1024 resolution, with competitive GenEval and DPG-Bench scores relative to much larger latent-diffusion T2I systems (e.g., FLUX-dev, DALLE-3), demonstrating practical scalability beyond class-conditional toy settings.

The image-editing experiment (FlowEdit, Table 14 and Fig. 1b) offers a compelling and practically relevant demonstration of a genuine advantage of pixel-space diffusion (avoiding VAE reconstruction artifacts), going beyond generic FID comparisons to show a concrete use case.

The appendix is unusually thorough and transparent: it includes extensive additional ablations (solver comparison, CFG scale/interval, depth allocation N/M, token-compaction rate, patch size at 512, REPA ablation), detailed architecture/training configs for reproducibility, a FLOPs/compute comparison table, and an honest "Things We Tried But Did Not Work" section, which is valuable both for reproducibility and for informing future research on pixel-space diffusion.
Code, models, and project page links are provided, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Despite the narrowed gap, the method still underperforms the strongest latent diffusion baselines reported in the same table (e.g., RAE-XL 1.13 FID, DDT-XL 1.26 FID vs. PixelDiT's 1.61), so claims of "approaching" or "closing much of the gap" to SOTA latent models should be read with this caveat; the paper is reasonably careful about this but a reader skimming the abstract could overstate the result.

The paper reports GFLOPs as the primary efficiency metric, but pixel-space training/inference wall-clock and memory costs (beyond the single throughput number at 512/1024) are not compared head-to-head against latent baselines under matched hardware/epochs, making it harder to assess the true practical training cost of adopting this approach at scale.

The T2I model is trained on an internal, non-released 26M image-text corpus at 1024 resolution; since this data is not public, exact reproduction of the T2I results is not fully possible from the paper alone despite code/model release.

The limitations section itself acknowledges that pixel-space training with velocity prediction is prone to loss spikes, particularly for deeper architectures and long runs, and that this remains only partially mitigated -- an unresolved training-stability concern relevant to anyone trying to extend or reproduce the approach at larger scale.

T2I comparisons include models of substantially larger parameter count (e.g., FLUX-dev/DALLE-3 at ~12B vs. PixelDiT-T2I at 1.3B); while the comparison is informative, the scale mismatch limits how much can be concluded about the architecture's efficiency advantage per se.

Evaluation is restricted to ImageNet class-conditional generation and a single internally curated T2I setting plus one editing benchmark (FlowEdit, 281 samples); broader benchmarks (e.g., other T2I benchmarks, human preference studies, more diverse editing datasets) would strengthen generality claims.
